valid: The main benefit of working from home is higher productivity. When employees no longer have to commute, they save time and energy, which in turn allows them to start work fresh and focused. For example, an accountant in Bangkok who used to spend two hours a day in traffic on Sukhumvit Road can use that time to finish reports before lunch, and her company receives more work for the same salary. However, some staff find it difficult to concentrate at home with children around. Even so, for most employees the hours saved on the journey make remote work more productive overall.

Working from home can make employees more productiv because it removes the daily journey to the office. Without a long commute, staff begin the day less tired, and this energy goes directly into their tasks. In Bangkok, for instance, a marketing officer at a small company in Silom might lose ninety minutes each morning on the BTS and in traffic; at home, he can answer emails by eight o’clock. Admittedly, not every employee has a quiet room, and some are distracted by family. Neverthless, for most workers the time saved is more valuable than these problems, so companies benefit as well.

The clearest advantage of remote work for a company is that its employees become more productive. The mechanism is simple: by cutting out commuting, home working gives people back several hours a week, and rested workers make fewer mistakes and finish tasks faster. A software firm in the Bang Na district of Bangkok reported that its programmers completed more projects after it allowed them to work from home three days a week, because they no longer arrived exhausted from traffic. It is true that some managers worry they cannot supervise staff at home. In reality, however, results can be measured by output rather than by hours at a desk, so this concern does not cancel the benefit.

One benefit of working from home is that employees is less stressed and therefore more productive. Long journeys in Bangkok traffic leave workers tired before the day even begins, whereas at home they can start immediatly and organise their time better. My aunt, who works for an insurance company in Ratchada, used to leave home at six in the morning; since her company let her work from home, she finishes her reports earlier and makes fewer errors. Of course, working alone can feel lonely, and some people miss their colleagues. However, in reality this can be solved by meeting in the office once a week, so the productivity benefit remains.

Home working raises productivity because it gives employees control over their environment. Instead of losing energy in crowded trains, staff can work in a quiet space at the hours when they concentrate best, which in turn improves the quality of their work. A clear example is a Bangkok bank’s call centre team, which handled more customer cases per day after the company moved them to home-based shifts during the rainy season floods. Admittedly, younger employees may learn more slowly without senior colleagues beside them. Even so, this is a reason to train them online, not a reason to abandon a system that makes the company more productive.

The most obvious benefit of working from home is the time it gives back to employees. By removing the daily commute, remote work frees two or three hours that staff can spend on focused tasks or on rest, which in turn makes them more productive when they sit down at their desks. A marketing company in Bangkok, for instance, found that its team completed projects faster after staff stopped spending the morning stuck on Sukhumvit Road. Admittedly, some employees feel isolated at home and miss chatting with colleagues; even so, a weekly office day can solve this without losing the gains in productivity.

Home-based work is beneficial mainly because it lets employees organize their day around their own energy. When an office worker is no longer forced into a fixed schedule, deep work can be planned for the hours in which concentration is highest, so output rises. This was seen at a small Thai software firm where programmers chose to work at home in the afternoons; the company reported fewer missed deadlines within six months. That said, not every job can be done from a laptop, and a cashier or a nurse cannot stay home. For desk-based roles, however, the productivity gain remains clear.

Working remotely also saves money for both staff and the company. An employee who stays at home no longer pays for petrol, parking or a BTS ticket, while the employer can rent a smaller office, and these savings can be reinvested in training that raises productivity. My aunt, an accountant in Nonthaburi, saves around 3,000 baht a month since her firm moved to a hybrid model, and her manager says the team’s output has not fallen. On the other hand, remote staff may find it harder to separate work from family life. Nevertheless, with clear working hours, the finacial benefit clearly outweighs this risk.

valid: The first reason to support a ban is that school is where eating habits are formed. Students buy snacks at the same time every day, so a sugary drink at break becomes a routine, and routines repeated for years turn into adult preferences. At a girls' school in Bangkok, for instance, students who bought a sweet iced tea every break often admitted that they still crave one every afternoon. It is true that students can still buy snacks from shops outside the school gate. However, the school controls the six hours a day when students eat most regularly, so removing sugary snacks there still breaks the routine where it starts.

When a teenager buys a chocolate bar from the canteen every morning, the sweet taste becomes normal, and this habit continues into adulthood, which increases the risk of obesity and diabetes. For example, at my old school in Nonthaburi, the canteen sold soft drinks at every break, and many of my classmates still drink two or three cans a day. Eating behavior learned at school tends to last, which is the strongest argument for banning sugary snacks. The process works through repetition: a snack eaten at the same break every day becomes a ritual, the ritual becomes a craving, and the craving follows the student into adult life, damaging her health. A Bangkok school that replaced its candy counter with fruit stalls found that, within one term, students chose mango and watermelon without complaint. Of course, sweets remain available from vendors outside the gate. Yet the school day is the one place where adults can shape what teenagers eat, so it should model the habit it wants students to keep.

Selling sugary snacks at school teaches students a habit that is hard to break. Because teenagers eat at school five days a week, whatever the canteen sells becomes their normal diet; over several years, this routine sets the taste for sugar that they carry into adulthood, where it contributes to weight gain and tooth decay. Consider a secondary school in Chiang Mai where students buy sweet milk tea every lunchtime: by Mathayom 6, many cannot finish a meal without a sugary drink. valid: Paid work builds skills that the classroom rarely teaches. A job puts a teenager in front of real customers and real deadlines, which in turn teaches responsibility, communication and how to manage money. For example, a sixteen-year-old who works weekends at a café in Siam must greet customers politely, handle cash accurately and arrive on time, and she quickly becomes more confident and independent. Admittedly, too many hours can damage a student's schoolwork. Even so, a job of eight to ten hours a week gives students these benefits without harming their studies, so work experience remains valuable.

The most important benefit of a part-time job is that it makes students more independant. When teenagers earn their own money, they have to decide how to spend and save it, and this teach them to plan ahead instead of asking their parents. A good example is a Grade 11 student in Khon Kaen who works at a noodle shop on Saturdays; she now pays her own phone bill and keeps a simple budget. Of course, if she worked every evening, her grades at school would suffer. However, with a limit on hours, the job builds responsability without taking away study time.

Work experience develops independence by giving students responsibilities that nobody else can complete for them. At school a teacher reminds them of every deadline, but at work a manager expects them to solve problems alone, and this pressure gradually builds self-reliance and practical skills such as teamwork. Consider a Thai student who spends her summer holiday working at a Central department store: she learns to deal with complaints, cooperate with older colleagues and manage her time between shifts. It is true that jobs can tire students during exam periods. Nevertheless, if work is limited to holidays or weekends, the independence it builds is worth more than the time it costs.

Part-time work teach students skills they will need in their future careers. Serving customers forces a teenager to speak clearly, stay calm under pressure and follow instructions, and these habits carry over into university and later jobs. For instance, a student in Bangkok who tutors younger children on weekends must prepare lessons, organize her schedule and communicate with parents, which makes her more mature than many of her classmates. Admittedly, a job can take time away from homework and school. However, as long as students work no more than a few hours a week, the skills they gain outweigh the small loss of study time.

A part-time job builds independence because it moves a teenager from being looked after to being relied upon. Once a manager depends on her to open the shop or count the cash, she learns punctuality and accountability, and these qualities spill over into her studies at school. A Mathayom 5 student who works Sunday shifts at a bakery in Chiang Mai, for example, now plans her week around both her shifts and her exams, something she never had to do before. Admittedly, students who work long hours often fall behind. Even so, a limit of around eight hours a week lets them gain this maturity without risking their grades; the job’s value lies in responsibility, not in long hours.

Paid work gives teenagers skills that school rarely teaches. A part-time job puts a student in front of real customers and real deadlines, which in turn teaches her to communicate politely, manage her time and solve problems without a teacher to ask. A sixteen-year-old who serves at a café in Siam Square on Saturdays, for instance, quickly learns to handle complaints and to count change accurately under pressure. valid: Making public transport free would cut congestion in the city. The policy works by removing the fare, which is the main reason many drivers still choose their cars; once a bus ride costs nothing, the cheapest option is also the cleaner one. We can see this in Tallinn, Estonia, where free transport for residents led more people to leave their cars at home. Admittedly, taxpayers who never use buses would help pay for the system. Even so, they also gain from clearer roads and cleaner air, so funding free transport through tax is fair.

The strongest reason to make public transport free is that it would reduce traffic in the city. This works by changing what is cheapest: when a train ride is free and parking is expensive, many commuters will stop driving becuase the train saves them money. We can see this in Luxembourg, which made all buses and trains free in 2020. Admittedly, the goverment must raise taxes to pay for the system, and some citizens will complain. Even so, the money saved on road repairs and health care from cleaner air would cover much of this cost.

Free public transportation, funded by tax, would make the city fairer for low-income workers. The mechanism is straightforward: fares take a much larger share of a cleaner's daily wage than of a manager's, so removing them works like a pay rise for the people who need it most. We can see this in Bangkok, where a worker traveling from Bang Bua Thong to Silom can spend over a hundred baht a day on transport. Admittedly, higher taxes affect everyone, including the poor. Even so, a progressive tax places most of the cost on wealthier residents.

Free public transport would reduce air pollution in the city. It works by making buses and trains more attractive than private cars, so fewer vehicles is on the road and fewer fumes are released. We can see this in Dunkirk, France, where the number of bus passengers rose sharply after fares were abolished and many drivers said they used their cars less. Admittedly, the city must use tax money to replace ticket income. Even so, cleaner air saves the public health system money, so the tax spent on free transport is partly paid back.

Abolishing fares would get more residents onto public transport, easing the city’s traffic. The mechanism is behavioural: a ticket price, however small, is a daily reminder of cost, and removing it makes the bus the default choice rather than the car. We can see this in Tallinn, where free travel for registered residents increased public transport use within its first year. Admittedly, someone must pay, and the money will come from local taxes. Even so, a city that spends tax on free transport rather than on wider roads gets more movement for every baht.

Making public transport free would draw drivers out of their cars. The scheme works by removing the cost barrier: once a bus ride costs nothing, it becomes cheaper than petrol and parking, so commuters switch, and congestion and emissions fall across the city.
